spec: Join a list of strings into a natural-language list using commas, with 'or' before the last item. Zero items produce an empty string, one item is returned as-is, two items are joined as 'A or B', and three or more items are joined with commas and an oxford comma before 'or', like 'A, B, or C'.

Join a list of strings into a natural-language list using commas, with the given conjunction word before the last item. Zero items produce an empty string, one item is returned as-is, two items are joined as 'A CONJ B', and three or more items use commas with an oxford comma before the conjunction, like 'A, B, CONJ C'.

Join a list of strings into a natural-language list with 'and' before the last item. If any item itself contains a comma, use semicolons as the separators instead of commas (to avoid ambiguity), otherwise use commas as normal; the oxford-style separator before 'and' follows the same rule for three or more items.
visible_tests: assert oxford_join_semicolon(['Tokyo, Japan', 'Paris, France']) == 'Tokyo, Japan and Paris, France'

spec: Convert each number in the given list to its string form, then join them into a natural-language list with commas and 'and' before the last item, following the standard oxford-comma rule (zero items give an empty string, one item is returned alone, two are joined with 'and', three or more use an oxford comma).

Join a list of strings into a natural-language list with commas and an oxford comma before 'and', exactly like a standard oxford-comma join for one, two, or three-or-more items. If the list is empty, return the given empty_word string instead of an empty string.
Wrap the given string in double quote characters. If the string already contains any double quote characters, escape each one by preceding it with a backslash before wrapping.
Wrap the given string in single quote characters. If the string already contains any single quote characters, escape each one by preceding it with a backslash before wrapping.
Wrap the given string with a leading left curly double-quote character (“) and a trailing right curly double-quote character (”), with no other changes to the string's contents.
visible_tests: assert smart_quotes('a quote inside " here') == '“a quote inside " here”'

spec: Wrap the given string by concatenating the given opening marker string before it and the given closing marker string after it, with no escaping or other modification of the original string.
Return the string wrapped in double quotes only if it contains a space character or a comma character; otherwise return the string unchanged.

Wrap the given string with the given non-negative number of double-quote characters on both the left and right side (level pairs of quotes total), with no escaping of any quotes already present in the string.

Given a string, apply CSV-style quoting: if it contains a comma, a double-quote character, or a newline character, wrap it in double quotes and double any internal double-quote characters (replace each " with two ""). If none of those characters are present, return the string unchanged.
Given a block of text, prefix every line (split on newline characters) with '> ' to render it as a markdown-style blockquote, then rejoin the lines with newline characters.

Draw a simple box of plus-sign corners, dash top and bottom borders, and pipe sides around a single word, with one space of padding on each side of the word. Return the three lines joined by newline characters: top border, then the padded word row, then the same border again.

Center the given word, surrounded by a single space on each side, within a line of the given total width, padding with the given fill character on both sides. If the width is not greater than the word plus its two surrounding spaces, the padded word (with its single spaces) is returned unchanged.

Draw a box of plus-sign corners, dash borders, and pipe sides around a single word, with the given number of padding spaces on each side of the word inside the box. Return the top border, the padded word row, and the bottom border joined by newline characters.

Draw a box made entirely of '#' characters around a single word: a top row of '#' characters exactly 4 longer than the word, a middle row of '# ' then the word then ' #', and the same top row repeated at the bottom. Return the three rows joined by newline characters.

Build a three-line banner around a single word: a border line made of '=' characters exactly 4 longer than the word, a middle line formatted as '= word =', and the same border line repeated at the bottom. Return the three lines joined by newline characters.

Draw a single-character-bordered box around a word using only the given character ch for both the border and the sides: the top row is ch repeated (word length plus 4) times, the middle row is ch, a space, the word, a space, then ch, and the bottom row repeats the top row. Return the three rows joined by newline characters.

Build a three-line title banner of the given total width: a border line of '-' characters spanning the full width, a middle line with the word centered using spaces to fill the width, and the same border line repeated at the bottom. Return the three lines joined by newline characters.

Format an integer n as a zero-padded string of at least the given width: pad with leading zeros so the digits occupy width characters, keeping a leading minus sign (not counted in the zero-padding of digits) for negative numbers. If str(n) is already at least width characters long, return it unchanged.
Given a string prefix, an integer n, and a padding width, return the prefix concatenated with n zero-padded to the given width, for example prefix 'INV-' with n 123 and width 6 becomes 'INV-000123'.
Given an integer n, a padding width, and a suffix string, return n zero-padded to the given width followed immediately by the suffix, for example n 42 with width 5 and suffix '-A' becomes '00042-A'.

Generate a list of count sequential ids starting at start, each formatted as the given prefix followed by the number zero-padded to width. For example prefix 'A-', start 1, count 3, width 3 produces ['A-001', 'A-002', 'A-003']. A count of 0 produces an empty list.

Zero-pad the integer n to the given width, then compute a check digit as the sum of the padded numeric digits modulo 10, and append that single check digit to the end. Negative numbers keep their zero-padded minus sign but the check digit is still based only on the digit characters.
Format a non-negative integer n as a lowercase hexadecimal string zero-padded on the left to at least the given width. For example n 255 with width 4 becomes '00ff'.

Zero-pad the non-negative integer n to the given width, then split the resulting digit string into consecutive chunks of the given group size (the last chunk may be shorter) and join the chunks with hyphens.

Given a digit-only id string (possibly zero-padded), strip its leading zeros; if the string was entirely zeros, treat the resulting value as '0'. Then re-pad the resulting digits to new_width with leading zeros. If new_width is smaller than the stripped digit count, the digits are returned unpadded and unshortened.

Split text into sentence fragments wherever '. ' (a period followed by a space) occurs. For each fragment, lowercase it and then uppercase its first alphabetic character (fragments with no letters stay fully lowered). Rejoin the fixed fragments with '. '.
visible_tests: assert sentence_case_multi('HELLO. HOW ARE you.') == 'Hello. How are you.'

spec: Split text on newline characters. For each non-empty line, lowercase it and then uppercase its first alphabetic character (a line with no letters stays fully lowered). Lines that are completely empty are left as empty strings. Rejoin all lines with newline characters.

Apply sentence casing to s (lowercase the whole string, then uppercase its first alphabetic character). Then split the result on single spaces and, for any word that matches (ignoring case) one of the given acronym strings, replace it with that acronym's exact given form; other words keep their sentence-cased form. Rejoin the words with single spaces.
visible_tests: assert sentence_case_preserve_acronyms('the nasa mission launched', ['NASA']) == 'The NASA mission launched'
assert sentence_case_preserve_acronyms('visit the usa today', ['USA']) == 'Visit the USA today'

spec: Collapse every run of whitespace in s into a single space and strip any leading or trailing whitespace, then lowercase the result and uppercase its first alphabetic character (if there is one).
visible_tests: assert fix_sentence_spacing('multiple   spaces   here') == 'Multiple spaces here'

spec: Lowercase the entire string, then uppercase the first alphabetic character of the string overall, and also uppercase the first alphabetic character that follows each occurrence of the substring ': ' (colon then space). Other characters remain lowercase.
visible_tests: assert capitalize_after_colon('NOTE: this is important') == 'Note: This is important'
assert capitalize_after_colon('WARNING: DANGER: proceed with care') == 'Warning: Danger: Proceed with care'
assert capitalize_after_colon('no colon here') == 'No colon here'

spec: Lowercase the whole string, then split it on single spaces and replace any word that is exactly the single letter 'i' with the uppercase letter 'I'. Rejoin the words with single spaces, then uppercase the first alphabetic character of the resulting string.
visible_tests: assert sentence_case_keep_i('i think this works') == 'I think this works'
assert sentence_case_keep_i('do YOU think i am right') == 'Do you think I am right'

spec: Return a version of the string where the first alphabetic character is lowercase and every other alphabetic character is uppercase; non-alphabetic characters are left unchanged. If the string has no alphabetic characters, return it fully lowercased.
Replace every character in the given filename that is not a letter, digit, hyphen, underscore, or period with an underscore, leaving allowed characters untouched.

First replace every space character in the filename with an underscore, then remove any remaining character that is not a letter, digit, underscore, period, or hyphen (do not replace them, just drop them).
Lowercase the filename and replace every space with a hyphen, then remove any character that is not a lowercase letter, digit, hyphen, or period.
Replace every run of two or more consecutive underscore characters in the filename with a single underscore, then strip any leading or trailing underscores from the result.

Build a filename slug from the given name: lowercase it, replace every run of one or more non-alphanumeric characters with a single hyphen, and strip any leading or trailing hyphens. Then truncate the result to at most max_len characters, and if that truncation leaves a trailing hyphen, strip it too.
